newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: BolsWes scam fuels need for new Dutch insider law.
newsitem.headline: BolsWes scam fuels need for new Dutch insider law.

text.p: Recent arrests in the year-long BolsWessanen insider dealing saga have increased the pressure on legislators to eliminate glaring loopholes in Dutch laws to combat insider trading.
Dutch finance ministry officials confirmed on Monday that a new bill to shore up holes in the existing Supervision of Securities Trading Act was currently being drafted.
With the seven-year old Dutch law on abuse of inside information yet to see a successful conviction, the BolsWessanen case is being closely watched in the Netherlands.

"The current law makes it difficult for the prosecutor to get the necessary evidence on the knowledge people have about a company," said Hans Van der Liet, a policy maker in the securities division at the Finance Ministry.
"The High Court here has ruled that the inside trader had to know from the beginning in what direction the securities would go which is difficult to prove," he said.
"It's also very difficult to prove whether the information was subject to secrecy or not. Now we're devising a law which is more lenient on these two counts."
He added the current law also has to prove the player conducted the dealings for personal gain, another requirement which will be scrapped under the new law.

In a major defeat for prosecutors last year, the Dutch supreme court annulled the insider trading conviction of entrepreneur Joep van den Nieuwenhuyzen, the former chairman of the Begemann NV industrial conglomerate.
The maximum sentence for insider trading in the Netherlands is a two year prison term or a 100,000 guilder ($59,100) fine. For corporations, the fine may be up to one million guilders.

The investigation into beleaguered food and drinks group BolsWessanen culminated in the arrest of five people recently, including a senior company executive identified only as T.J. Van N, director of business development.
The investigation was sparked by exceptionally heavy trading in BolsWessanen put options on July 3, 1995. The next day, the firm announced a steep profit drop.
But analysts said the news was no reason for investors to jump ship.
"I think we've seen the trough in the insider dealing case (in BolsWessanen) and all the bad news associated with it," said ING Barings analyst Gerard Rijk.

"It's disappointing that someone inside the company is involved, but investors look to the future," he said. "The company is still holding its full year forecast so that might give some positive sentiment," he added.
-- Jennifer Scott, Amsterdam newsroom +31 20 504 5000 ($ = 1.69 Dutch Guilders)
